title: Fred Trump’s FHA Financing for Shore Haven and Beach Haven
description_short: Fred Trump’s FHA Financing for Shore Haven and Beach Haven
description_medium: TrumpFile’s timeline reports that Fred Trump bought Virginia Beach property for Beach Haven apartments intended for Navy personnel in January 1945. It says the FHA provided $10.4 million for Shore Haven by dividing funding among three land purchases despite a $5 million project-financing limit, and claims FHA funding for the first two complexes exceeded construction costs by at least $3.5 million. The linked page attributes these claims to an FHA investigation and a Wayne Barrett excerpt; the linked 2018 New York Times interactive could not be read.
description_long: TrumpFile’s timeline entry, dated January 12, 1945 and updated August 9, 2020, reports that Fred Trump acquired Virginia Beach property for Beach Haven apartments intended for Navy personnel. The page says the FHA provided $10.4 million for Shore Haven through three separate land purchases despite a $5 million limit on government-project financing, and claims that FHA-backed funding for the first two complexes exceeded their construction costs by at least $3.5 million. It cites an “FHA Investigation,” page 52, and an excerpt from Wayne Barrett’s book. These are claims in the linked account; its linked New York Times interactive from October 2018 returned HTTP 403 and could not be checked. TrumpFile does not reproduce the loan records, identify the FHA officials involved, provide terms for each project, or document political maneuvering. This account therefore attributes the reported amounts and comparison to TrumpFile without treating them as proof of improper intent.
notes: Focused read of the supplied TrumpFile page (timeline date January 12, 1945; page updated August 9, 2020) supplies the specific claims: Shore Haven FHA funding of $10.4 million across three land purchases, a stated $5 million financing limit, and an asserted $3.5 million excess over construction costs for the first two complexes. It also says the Beach Haven property was intended for Navy apartments and cites an FHA investigation, p. 52, and a Wayne Barrett excerpt. The linked New York Times interactive returned HTTP 403. The linked TrumpFile page does not provide loan instruments, separate project terms, named FHA decision-makers, or evidence of political maneuvering; the description attributes the claims and omits the latter assertions.

title: Mogilevich Establishes Budapest Business Base; TrumpFile Notes Associate at Trump Tower
description_short: Mogilevich Establishes Budapest Business Base; TrumpFile Notes Associate at Trump Tower
description_medium: TrumpFile’s March 1, 1991 timeline says Semion Mogilevich moved to Hungary after marrying Katalin Papp and began investing in local businesses, naming Magnex, Digep, and Army Co-op. It also says that by 1993, associate Vyacheslav Ivankov had been found living in Trump Tower. A September 11, 1999 New York Times report describes Mogilevich as a reputed Russian organized-crime leader and reports that he denied links to the Benex money-laundering investigation. Neither source establishes Donald Trump’s personal involvement in the Budapest activity.
description_long: TrumpFile’s timeline entry, dated March 1, 1991 and updated May 3, 2021, says Semion Mogilevich moved to Hungary after marrying Katalin Papp and invested in Hungarian businesses. It names Magnex 2000, Digep General Machine Works, and Army Co-op, and says a holding company called Arigon owned 95 percent of Army Co-op. The page also reports that by 1993 Vyacheslav Ivankov, described as one of Mogilevich’s partners, was found living in Trump Tower. This is the source’s indirect connection to the Trump chronology; it does not show that Donald Trump knew Ivankov or participated in Mogilevich’s Budapest operations. A September 11, 1999 New York Times report says U.S. and European authorities described Mogilevich as a major Russian organized-crime leader and suspected a link to possible laundering through Benex. Mogilevich denied knowing or dealing with Benex. That report addresses the investigation, not his Budapest move or Ivankov’s residence.
notes: Focused reads: TrumpFile’s March 1, 1991 timeline page (updated May 3, 2021) reports the move to Hungary, marriage, business investments, named companies, and says Mogilevich associate Vyacheslav Ivankov was found living in Trump Tower by 1993. The September 11, 1999 New York Times article, “Reputed Russian Mobster Denies Tie To Laundering, and Takes Umbrage,” says authorities described Mogilevich as a major organized-crime leader and suspected a possible Benex money-laundering link; Mogilevich denied knowing or dealing with Benex. The NYT article does not address Budapest or Trump Tower, and neither linked source establishes Donald Trump’s personal involvement. The corrected entry confines the Trump connection to the reported associate/property link and does not state the page’s unsubstantiated theft or KGB claims as fact.

title: Litvinenko Alleges FSB Assassination Plot and Mafia Control at Press Conference
description_short: Litvinenko Alleges FSB Assassination Plot and Mafia Control at Press Conference
description_medium: TrumpFile’s November 17, 1998 timeline says former FSB officer Alexander Litvinenko and other security officials held a press conference. It reports that Litvinenko accused his superiors of plotting to assassinate Boris Berezovsky and that the speakers alleged organized crime controlled the Russian government. Those are attributed allegations, not findings established by the event. The page says Vladimir Putin did not attend and Litvinenko was arrested and left Russia months later. It does not connect the press conference to Donald Trump.
description_long: TrumpFile’s timeline entry, dated November 17, 1998 and updated March 11, 2021, describes a press conference by former FSB officer Alexander Litvinenko and other Russian security officials. The page says Litvinenko accused his superiors of plotting to assassinate businessman Boris Berezovsky and that the speakers alleged Russian government institutions and organized crime were intertwined. It also says Vladimir Putin, then FSB director, did not attend, and that Litvinenko was arrested and left Russia months later. The allegations are what the participants reportedly said; the press conference itself does not establish that the alleged assassination plot or asserted mafia control was true. The other supplied link is a Washington Post article dated October 2, 1997 about the FBI director and Russian organized-crime threats; the page request timed out, and its date predates the press conference. Neither supplied source shows why this 1998 event belongs in a Trump-focused record or establishes a Trump connection.
notes: Focused read of the supplied TrumpFile page (November 17, 1998 event; updated March 11, 2021) confirms that it reports Litvinenko and other security officials held a press conference, attributes an assassination-plot allegation to Litvinenko, and attributes claims of mafia control to the speakers. It also says Putin did not attend and that Litvinenko was later arrested and left Russia. These remain source-reported allegations, not verified findings. The supplied Washington Post link is dated October 2, 1997 and concerns the FBI director and Russian organized-crime threats; the request timed out and it predates the event. Neither link establishes a Trump connection. Still needed: evidence of the event-specific Trump relevance to retain the entry in this chronology.

title: Trump File Claims Manafort Helped Russia Take Crimea, Without Details
description_short: Trump File Claims Manafort Helped Russia Take Crimea, Without Details
notes: Focused read of the supplied TrumpFile entry confirms only its March 16, 2014 assertion that Russia took control of Crimea “with help from Paul Manafort” through an “illegal vote”; the page says it would add more details and cites a Vox Ukraine explainer. The page supplies no date or act by Manafort, no explanation of what assistance he provided, and no evidence linking his actions to the takeover. The Vox page is mentioned within TrumpFile but is not one of this row’s supplied source URLs. Still needed: source evidence identifying a specific Manafort action and its connection to Russia’s control of Crimea, or correction that removes the attribution.
